name: Dana Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What machine do you run?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 58, and I run a wood-panel router that cuts cabinet doors. I earned a vocational machine-operations certificate and have spent thirteen years on this line. I can set a normal door pattern and catch a chipped edge, but a technician repairs the spindle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your home finances and your habits with AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ruth sells supplies at a builders' merchant, and our grown children live on their own. My early-shift allowance makes my operator wage higher than usual, we've saved about ten months of expenses, and there are plenty of furniture and cabinet shops nearby. I use AI now and then to understand a manual update, but I follow the approved router sheet and measure a real door. I trust paid apprenticeships and steady work more than an untested promise of support. Ruth and I have not yet compared written retirement income with our living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can quote cabinet orders more quickly if the door measurements still reach my bench correctly. I would keep the first cut panel until the caliper agrees with the drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The router still needs an operator, and our current wages plus ten months saved cover the bills. A faster office quote is not a reason to throw away a good machine routine. I would be pleased if fewer wrong drawings reach the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the router to the approved sheet, measure the first door after each pattern change and mark any chipped panel for the lead. I would keep using AI only occasionally for manual notices, after checking them with the technician. If a full paid month leaves money after bills, Ruth and I would put new wage money into our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tidy quote is useful, but the customer takes home the door, not the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check the first door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I measure the hinge holes and the outside width against the paper drawing. If the edge chips, I stop the cutter and ask the technician to check the tool before the batch runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add to savings when you have ten months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The early allowance might not last through retirement. I mean a new amount from future full paid wages after household costs, not a new name for money already saved.

The first **cut panel** stays until a caliper check passes.
think: Current **shift wages** and ten months saved cover the bills.
The **router routine** remains useful while office work speeds up.
do: **Keep** cutting and measuring first cabinet doors after pattern changes.
**Check** occasional AI manual notices with the technician before use.
**Save** new wages from full paid months after household costs.
feel: **Calm** because present machine work and household pay remain sound.

fieldNote: Her **mid-level machine experience** covers ordinary patterns and quality checks, while spindle repair stays with a technician.

steps.text: Keep cutting and measuring first cabinet doors after pattern changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the floor that software might schedule board orders before robots can lift and cut the doors. If the plant wants an AI edge camera, show me its guarded test and the early-shift roster together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am open to a camera after somebody proves it catches a chipped edge. My concern is that faster work could merge shifts and take away the allowance that lifts my wage. Ten months saved and Ruth's shop pay give us time, but a lower regular wage would change our retirement sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the proposed early roster with my last four wage slips and ask for a paid guarded camera trial run by the technician. If offered a supervised practice place, I would learn the AI edge-alert screen on good and chipped scrap doors, checking each alert with a caliper before changing the approved cut. If paid hours actually fall, I would apply only to posted safe local cabinet-machine jobs whose guaranteed base wage after travel and shifts covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible lost allowance, even though the camera could be useful. A paid trial is worth my time; a shortened payslip is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the scrap trial prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feed one door with a deliberately chipped edge and one clean door under the guard. The technician and I would compare the camera flag with the measured edge before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another shop have to offer the same shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could offer a different shift, but the posted guaranteed rate after travel must still meet our costs. I would not rely on a possible production bonus.

A **chipped scrap door** should test camera alerts.
think: Merged **early shifts** could remove my higher allowance.
Ten months **saved** and Ruth's pay cannot replace a permanently lower rate.
do: **Compare** proposed early hours with four wage slips.
**Learn** AI edge alerts only if paid guarded supervised scrap practice is offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe local cabinet work at bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic loss of higher shift income.
S1.quote: A paid trial is worth my time; a shortened payslip is not.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** requires offered hands-on paid guarded camera practice, beyond occasional manual-notice reading.

steps.text: Compare proposed early roster with four pay slips and request guarded trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth that AGI might quote cabinet orders in 2028, while capable robots to load and cut doors arrive around 2031. The factory should say which paid shop jobs remain before the robot router is ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots can handle the physical panels. I expect many router shifts, perhaps mine, to go, and another furniture plant might be installing the same machines. Our ten-month reserve gives us a search window, but I would miss the higher early rate if I had to start elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would defer our planned patio repair while it is still safe and hold that money for household bills. I would take a locally accepted cabinet-quality course only if an actual funded place provides paid release and guarded supervised router practice. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local quality roles only if guaranteed wages after travel and shift times meet our costs; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe cabinet-machine jobs on the same terms while keeping any offered paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing a good wage, though savings and nearby shops give us room to compare. I would rather earn a practical certificate than wait for a promised handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical course work include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a door, reject a chipped edge and isolate the router before changing a cutter. A trainer should watch me behind the guard, not tick off a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire instead of changing jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income and Ruth's dependable wages cover housing, food and health costs. We have not checked that sum, so I would pursue paid work first.

The plant should list **remaining paid jobs** before ordering a robot line.
think: At **63**, the early-rate router shift may disappear.

do: **Defer** the safe patio repair and keep cash for bills.

**Apply** after cuts to posted safe quality if qualified, or cabinet fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about replacing a higher wage despite a strong cushion.
S2.quote: I would rather earn a practical certificate than wait for a promised handout.
fieldNote: Her **2031 risk** is robots handling physical doors after AGI first changes order quotations.
Both **quality and cabinet searches** depend on actual safe local postings and bill-covering guaranteed wages after travel.

steps.text: Defer planned patio repair while safe and retain cash for bills
Take accepted quality course only if funded paid guarded router practice offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might quote cabinet work in 2031 while capable robots reach the router around 2034. Five years is enough to see which nearby shops accept a practical quality certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 then. Ruth and I could decide to stop if written retirement income covers our costs, but I will not assume the allowance has somehow become a guaranteed payment. The current high wage and ten months saved let me check a real course before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement estimates against our housing and health costs this year. If we still need my wage, I would enrol in a cabinet-quality certificate only when local shops accept it and a funded place includes paid release plus guarded supervised router practice. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if guaranteed base pay after travel and shift hours covers bills; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe cabinet-machine jobs on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about whether the numbers support stopping work, though our bills are sound today. I would like a trade I can prove on a real door, not a pile of course brochures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test local acceptance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the certificate name with actual nearby quality postings and ask the hiring shops if guarded router practice counts. If they say no, I would stay on the paid shift and look for a course they do accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave work before 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If written retirement income and Ruth's reliable wage cover housing, food, travel and health costs, I would leave before the robot change. If they do not, I would keep working or apply for a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could quote cabinet work in 2036, while capable robots reach the physical router around 2039. Ten years gives us time to judge whether I still need the early shift at that point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when those robots arrive, if I am still employed. Our current wage and ten-month reserve make near-term living secure, and Ruth and I hope to stop before the machines take over. We need written retirement income that covers housing and health costs before making the decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working safe paid router shifts and request written retirement-income estimates beside a full household cost list this year. If the figures show I still need wages, I would take an accepted cabinet-quality course only if fees, paid release and guarded supervised practice are funded. If I remain at work after 2036 and shifts fall, I would apply only to posted safe local cabinet jobs with guaranteed pay after travel and shift times that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long end, but not worried about today's groceries. I want the household figures settled before giving up a useful wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the retirement comparison?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I would put written income beside housing, food, transport and likely health costs. Our grown children have their own responsibilities, so I would not treat their earnings as our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you never take the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep any safe paid router shift and look at actual local cabinet postings if hours fall. I would not buy a certificate a hiring shop does not accept.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture would test us most because it could take my better-paid early router shift before retirement sums are known. A funded practical quality place accepted by cabinet shops, posted safe local jobs at enough pay after travel, and written staffing dates would help. I would keep the paid shift until one of those is real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the chipped doors after the machine reports a complete batch. A door with a broken edge is still a broken door in someone's kitchen.

headlineQuote: A door with a broken edge is still a broken door in someone's kitchen.
portrait: **Dana**, 58, is an experienced mid-level cabinet-door router operator with a vocational certificate and average machine skill.
She and her **partner Ruth** have grown children, higher early-shift pay, ten months saved and plenty of cabinet shops nearby.
She uses **AI occasionally** for manual notices, favours proven machine routines and values practical paid apprenticeships.
Possible **2031 physical robots** threaten a good wage; an earlier stop depends on written retirement income covering costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 router robots** could remove her higher paid early shift before a viable replacement wage or retirement sum is established.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **accepted funded practical training**, posted safe local cabinet jobs at workable net pay and written staffing dates.
